verdict.reasoning: Patient reports anxiety for 'about two months or so' with 'really nervous every morning about leaving the house,' palpitations ('my heart kind of racing') and poor sleep ('I can't get to sleep for hours and hours and hours').

She states symptoms have been present 'about two months or so' and that this 'probably coincides with me starting a new job... quite stressful' in a retail head office, and later notes 'I have felt it get worse and worse over the past.'

Morning palpitations: 'I find my heart kind of racing... I wake up in a panic.' Irregular: Doctor asks 'regular fast beat or an irregular beat?' and she replies 'Irregular, I think.' Duration: 'a couple of minutes' up to '10 minutes.' Chest pain: she says 'No. Well, yeah, it's painful when... my heart is being fat,' consistent with no distinct chest pain apart from the sensation of forceful beating.

Insomnia: goes to bed 'About 10, 11,' 'I can't get to sleep for hours and hours and hours,' total sleep 'maybe three, four hours I'm getting now,' and she wakes early with 'my heart kind of racing' and 'find myself waking up before [the alarm].'

Low energy: 'It's just really, really low.' Loss of interest and avoidance: she 'find[s] no enjoyment at all... anything that previously was really fun is just not enjoyable,' avoids friends ('I avoid them... I know that I'm not going to have fun') and is doing hobbies such as running and tennis 'not quite so much.'

Low mood: 'I'm pretty much down... constant feeling of just being a bit down, a bit unhappy.' Denies suicidal ideation: 'I haven't had any suicidal thoughts or any thoughts that have been that extreme.'

She says 'Probably not significant changes... I wouldn't say I'm eating much differently.' but adds 'I probably have more chocolate than normal just because I feel so down,' indicating stable appetite with more chocolate.
No past medical or surgical history is mentioned anywhere in the transcript, so stating that it was not discussed is consistent with the record.
The transcript does not mention any current medications or explicitly say she takes none; therefore asserting she takes no medications introduces new information.
Allergies are not mentioned anywhere in the consultation, so stating that allergies were not discussed matches the absence of such information.
She says 'I talked to my mum because she also suffers from, or she's suffered from like depression in the past,' indicating maternal history of depression.
When asked who she lives with, she answers 'Yeah, I live with my parents. With my parents.'

She reports 'probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday day... I probably go over my limit just on those days anyway. And then like maybe a glass of wine during the week.' The transcript does not quantify this as 'more than approximately 14 units per week' or explicitly describe bingeing; that numerical estimate is inferred and not stated.
She says 'I try not to smoke, but I do occasionally, but I don't take them' in response to 'Do you smoke or take any other drugs or anything?', indicating occasional smoking and no drug use.
She states 'I work for a fashion retailer in the head office team' and 'My boss is not very nice to me.'
The clinician comments, 'I can see that you're quite distressed by it,' indicating the patient appears visibly distressed/anxious.

The anxiety is clearly work-related ('majority of it is focused around work') and of 2 months duration. While 'generalized anxiety disorder' is not named, the clinician frames it as 'some people with anxiety... need to take medication,' consistent with assessing an anxiety disorder driven largely by work stress.

Insomnia is temporally and causally linked to anxiety about work ('I can't get to sleep for hours... so stressed and so worried' and waking with panic about being late). The doctor also plans information 'about helping with your sleep patterns' as part of anxiety management, consistent with insomnia secondary to anxiety.

Doctor says 'In terms of palpitations, it is most likely to be associated with anxiety, but it's probably worth having a couple of basic blood tests just to make sure that there's not something triggering that off,' indicating likely anxiety-related with organic causes to be excluded.

Doctor states 'you can self refer via the NHS for what we call like talking therapy, which is a type of behavioral therapy... So I can send you the link for that,' consistent with self-referral to CBT-style talking therapy.

Doctor: 'there are some online resources that are really helpful. Put the details on there and you can get on with them straight away' and 'I'll put some more information on your notes about helping with your sleep patterns and things like that,' matching online anxiety resources and sleep hygiene advice.
Doctor mentions 'a couple of basic blood tests' but does not specify full blood count, urea and electrolytes, or thyroid function tests; naming these specific tests adds unstated detail.
Doctor instructs, 'So if you call this line, you can arrange the. Have the blood test done,' indicating the patient should call to arrange blood tests.
Doctor says 'arranging a GP follow up a week after you've had the test so we can just go through the results with you,' which is a GP review planned one week after blood tests.

Doctor advises, 'if you're feeling like it's not helping at all or your anxiety is getting worse to the point where you can't cope with work... give us a call back and just discuss that further,' and adds 'some people with anxiety, they do need to take medication... that's not something that we suggest in the first instance,' implying medication will be considered if therapy/other measures are ineffective and symptoms or functioning worsen; suicidal ideation is already screened and would also warrant return.
As above, 'arranging a GP follow up a week after you've had the test' describes follow-up one week after blood tests.

He says to call back if 'your anxiety is getting worse to the point where you can't cope with work or you can't just do your normal things day to day,' which corresponds to worsening symptoms or functional impairment; given earlier explicit denial of suicidal thoughts, emergent suicidal ideation would logically be a reason to return as well.
